title: Agile & Scrum in Practice
subtitle: Run real Sprints, from an ordered backlog and capacity-based planning to Reviews and Retrospectives that change how a team works.
description: A practical, advanced course on Agile values and the Scrum framework exactly as the 2020 Scrum Guide defines it, with Kanban for flow-based work. You will set up a backlog and board, facilitate every Scrum event, read burndown charts, diagnose struggling teams and build the evidence and certification plan for Scrum Master or delivery roles.
outcomes: Explain Agile values and the Scrum accountabilities, events and artifacts accurately
Set up an ordered Product Backlog, a Sprint board and a Definition of Done
Plan a Sprint from real capacity and velocity, and facilitate the Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective
Read a burndown chart and use Little's Law to spot and fix flow problems
Diagnose a team with interviews and a scored health check, and scope coaching work
Produce a case study and a 90-day plan toward a Scrum certification or role
audience: Women who already work in or alongside digital, project or programme teams and want to run or confidently contribute to Agile and Scrum work.
tools: Smartphone or laptop with internet access
A free Trello or Jira account, or Google Sheets
Google Forms (free) for anonymous health checks
Notebook and pen, or sticky notes, for planning and Retrospectives
A real or mock team of 3 to 7 people (friends, colleagues or volunteers)

modules.title: How Agile and Scrum Really Work
modules.overview: You start with the problem Agile solves and the four values and twelve principles behind it. Then you learn the Scrum framework exactly as its official guide defines it, and finally how to choose between Scrum, Kanban and a hybrid for a real team.

lessons.title: From fixed plans to short cycles: the Agile Manifesto in practice
objectives: Explain the difference between a plan-driven (waterfall) project and an iterative, Agile one
Name the four values of the Agile Manifesto and say what each means in daily work
Use the idea of an empirical process (inspect, then adapt) to judge when Agile fits
Calculate how much rework a late discovery costs compared with an early one

blocks.text: Picture a team building an online fees portal for a group of private schools in Abuja. In a **plan-driven** project, often called **waterfall**, they gather every requirement in month one, design in month two, build for three months and test at the end. The school owners see nothing usable until month six. If an important assumption was wrong, for example that parents would pay by card when most actually pay by bank transfer or USSD, the team learns it very late, after building the wrong thing.

An **Agile** team works in short cycles, usually one to four weeks. At the end of each cycle they have a small, working piece of the product that real users can try. They show it, collect feedback and adjust the plan. The same wrong assumption is discovered in week two, not month six.

blocks.name: idea-to-plan
blocks.alt: A person turning an idea into a step-by-step plan
blocks.caption: Agile turns one big, distant plan into many small plans that are checked against reality.

blocks.text: The Agile Manifesto: four values
In February 2001, seventeen software practitioners met in Snowbird, Utah, USA, and wrote the **Manifesto for Agile Software Development**. It is short. It says they have come to value:

head: We value more...
...than
What it looks like in practice
rows: Individuals and interactions
Processes and tools
A quick call to clear a confusion beats a long ticket thread
Working software
Comprehensive documentation
Progress is measured by what works, not by pages written
Customer collaboration
Contract negotiation
The client sees the product often and helps shape it
Responding to change
Following a plan
The plan is updated whenever the team learns something new

blocks.text: Read the last line of the manifesto carefully: "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more." Agile does **not** mean no documentation, no plan and no contract. It means those things serve the work, not the other way round. A common misunderstanding in workplaces is to use "we are Agile" as an excuse for no planning at all. That is not Agile, it is chaos.
A few of the twelve principles you will use most

items: **Deliver working software frequently**, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, preferring the shorter timescale.
**Welcome changing requirements**, even late in development, because change can give the customer an advantage.
**Business people and developers must work together daily** throughout the project.
**Working software is the primary measure of progress.**
**At regular intervals, the team reflects** on how to become more effective, then adjusts its behaviour.
**Simplicity**, the art of maximising the amount of work not done, is essential.

blocks.title: Agile beyond software
blocks.text: The manifesto was written for software, but the same ideas now guide marketing teams, programme teams in NGOs, content studios and event planners. Wherever the work is uncertain and feedback is possible, short cycles help. You will see this applied to non-software teams throughout this course.
Why short cycles work: empiricism

Agile rests on an **empirical** approach: knowledge comes from experience, and decisions are made on what is actually observed. You make a small step, **inspect** the result, and **adapt**. This is the right approach when the work is complex, meaning you cannot know everything in advance. When the work is simple and repeatable, such as printing 500 identical certificates, a fixed plan is perfectly fine.

blocks.title: Plan-driven versus Agile delivery
items: Plan-driven (waterfall)
Agile (iterative)
blocks.caption: Both approaches plan; the difference is how often the plan meets reality.

blocks.title: Worked example: the cost of a late discovery
blocks.context: For example, a team of 4 developers is building the school fees portal. Each developer costs the company about ₦25,000 per working day (approximate, illustrative figure). The card-payment assumption is wrong, and fixing it means rebuilding the payment flow.
steps: Waterfall case: the error is found in testing after 60 working days. Suppose 30% of the work built so far depends on the card assumption. Rework = 30% of 60 days = 18 days for the team.
Agile case: parents try the first working payment screen at the end of sprint 1 (10 working days). Only about 3 days of team work depend on the wrong assumption.
Difference = ₦1,800,000 − ₦300,000 = ₦1,500,000 saved, plus about two months of delay avoided.
blocks.result: Finding the wrong assumption in week two instead of month three cut the rework cost to one sixth. The numbers are illustrative, but the pattern is the core argument for short cycles.

blocks.title: Say it simply
blocks.text: In an interview, a strong one-line answer is: "Agile means delivering value in small, working pieces, checking them with real users often, and changing the plan based on what we learn."

takeaways: Agile replaces one distant delivery with frequent, working deliveries and regular feedback
The manifesto has four values; items on the right still matter, just less
Empiricism means inspect what really happened, then adapt
Late discovery of a wrong assumption is far more expensive than early discovery

activity.title: Practice task: spot the late discovery
steps: Think of a project you have seen (work, church, community, school, family event) that went off track.
Write down the wrong assumption and the week it was discovered.
Estimate how many days of work had to be redone, and in which week it could have been found with a short cycle.
Rewrite the project as 2-week cycles: what working piece could have been shown at the end of cycle 1?
activity.evidence: A one-page note (or phone photo of a handwritten page) with the assumption, the rework estimate and your cycle 1 piece.

lessons.title: The Scrum framework: three accountabilities, five events, three artifacts
objectives: Describe the Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers and what each is accountable for
List the five Scrum events with their official maximum timeboxes
Explain the three artifacts and the commitment attached to each
Map a two-week sprint onto a real team calendar

blocks.text: Agile is a set of values. **Scrum** is one specific, lightweight framework that puts those values to work, and it is the most widely used one. It is defined in a free, short document called **The Scrum Guide**, written by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. The current version is from November 2020. Everything in this lesson follows that guide, so you can check it yourself at scrumguides.org.
The Scrum Team: three accountabilities
A Scrum Team is small, **typically 10 or fewer people**, with no sub-teams and no hierarchy inside it. It has three accountabilities (the 2020 guide uses this word instead of "roles"):

head: Accountability
Accountable for
Common mistake
rows: Product Owner (one person)
Maximising the value of the product; ordering the Product Backlog; the Product Goal
Acting as a committee, or being too busy to answer questions
Scrum Master
The team's effectiveness; helping everyone understand Scrum; removing impediments
Behaving as a task manager who assigns work
Developers
Creating a usable Increment every Sprint; the Sprint Backlog; quality via the Definition of Done
Thinking "developer" means only programmers; testers, designers and writers are Developers too

blocks.name: scrum-board
blocks.alt: A team standing around a board of task cards
blocks.caption: The Scrum Team plans and tracks its own work; nobody outside assigns tasks to individuals.

blocks.text: Two details are worth remembering. The Product Owner is **one person, not a committee**; others may influence the backlog, but they do it by convincing the Product Owner. And the Scrum Master is a **leader who serves** the team and the wider organisation: coaching, facilitating when asked, and pushing to remove blockers that the team cannot remove alone, such as a slow approval process in another department.
The three pillars and five values

Scrum is built on three pillars: **transparency** (the work and progress are visible to all), **inspection** (the team checks progress often) and **adaptation** (it adjusts as soon as something is off). The guide also names five values: **commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage**. Courage matters more than people expect: it takes courage to say in a review that a feature is not finished.
The five events and their timeboxes

A **timebox** is a maximum duration. The guide gives maximums for a one-month Sprint and says shorter Sprints usually have shorter events. Many teams scale them in proportion, which gives the right-hand column.

head: Event
Purpose
Maximum for a 1-month Sprint
Common practice for 2 weeks
rows: The Sprint
Container for all other events; fixed length
One month or less
2 weeks (10 working days)
Sprint Planning
Why is this Sprint valuable, what can be Done, how will it get done
8 hours
About 4 hours
Daily Scrum
Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan
15 minutes every working day
15 minutes
Sprint Review
Inspect the outcome with stakeholders and decide what to do next
4 hours
About 2 hours
Sprint Retrospective
Plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness
3 hours
About 1.5 hours

blocks.title: One Scrum Sprint
items: Sprint Planning
Daily Scrum (every day)
Sprint Review
Sprint Retrospective
Next Sprint starts
blocks.caption: A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends, so the cycle never pauses.

blocks.text: The three artifacts and their commitments

items: **Product Backlog**: the ordered list of everything that might improve the product. Its commitment is the **Product Goal**, the long-term objective.
**Sprint Backlog**: the Sprint Goal, the items chosen for this Sprint, and the plan for delivering them. Its commitment is the **Sprint Goal**.

**Increment**: a usable step toward the Product Goal. Its commitment is the **Definition of Done**. Work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment and is not shown as finished.

blocks.text: Two more rules are often tested in certification exams. First, **only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint**, and only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Second, the 2020 guide no longer prescribes the famous "three questions" for the Daily Scrum: the Developers may use any structure, as long as the meeting focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal.

blocks.title: Worked example: placing a 2-week Sprint on a calendar
blocks.context: For example, Amaka is Scrum Master for a 6-person team (1 Product Owner, 5 Developers) at a Lagos logistics startup. Sprints run Monday to Friday of the following week.
steps: Day 1, Monday 10:00 to 14:00: Sprint Planning (4 hours, with a lunch break inside the box).
Days 1 to 10, every day at 09:30: Daily Scrum, 15 minutes, standing at the board or on a video call.
Day 10, Friday 10:00 to 12:00: Sprint Review with the operations manager and two riders who use the app.
Day 10, Friday 13:00 to 14:30: Sprint Retrospective, team only.
Total planned event time per person: 4 + (10 × 0.25) + 2 + 1.5 = 10 hours out of about 80 working hours.
blocks.result: About 12.5% of the Sprint goes to Scrum events. The rest, about 70 hours per person, is for doing and refining the work. Knowing this number helps when managers ask "why so many meetings?"

blocks.title: Old wording you will still hear
blocks.text: Many teams still say "Development Team", "standup" and "ceremonies". These are informal or older terms. In exams and formal writing, use the 2020 terms: Developers, Daily Scrum and events.

takeaways: Scrum has three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers
Five events, each timeboxed; the Daily Scrum is 15 minutes
Three artifacts, each with a commitment: Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done
Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint

activity.title: Practice task: build your Sprint calendar
steps: Pick a real or mock team of 4 to 7 people and choose a 1-week or 2-week Sprint length.
Write each Scrum event into a calendar (Google Calendar or paper) with times inside the timebox.
Add up the total event hours per person and the percentage of the Sprint they take.
Write one sentence for each accountability naming who would hold it in your team.
activity.evidence: A screenshot or photo of the calendar plus your calculation of event hours.

lessons.title: Scrum, Kanban or hybrid: choosing the right approach for the work
objectives: Explain how Kanban manages flow with visible work and work-in-progress (WIP) limits
Use Little's Law to estimate how long items take to finish
Choose Scrum, Kanban or a plan-driven approach for a given type of work
Identify where Agile skills are used in African and remote teams

blocks.text: Scrum is not the only Agile approach, and it is not always the best one. A good practitioner can look at a team's work and say which approach fits. The main alternative you will meet is **Kanban**.
Kanban in one page

Kanban (a Japanese word meaning "signboard") comes from manufacturing and was adapted for knowledge work. It has no Sprints and no fixed roles. Instead, the team makes its work visible on a board, **limits how much work is in progress at once**, and manages the flow of items from start to finish. New work can be pulled in at any time, as soon as there is space.

items: **Visualise the workflow**: columns such as To do, Doing, Review, Done.
**Limit work in progress (WIP)**: for example, no more than 3 cards in Doing. When the column is full, you finish something before starting something new.
**Measure flow**: how many items finish per day or week (throughput) and how long each takes from start to finish (cycle time).
**Improve continuously**: review the board regularly and remove bottlenecks.

blocks.name: work-in-progress
blocks.alt: A person moving cards across a progress board
blocks.caption: Kanban's main lever is limiting how much is in progress so that work actually finishes.

blocks.text: Little's Law: why WIP limits speed things up

A result from queueing theory called **Little's Law** says that, for a stable system, average cycle time = average work in progress ÷ average throughput. In plain words: if your team finishes the same number of items per day, having more items open at once makes each one take longer.

blocks.title: Worked example: a support team drowning in open tickets
blocks.context: For example, Funmi leads a customer support team at a payments company in Lagos. On average 30 complaint tickets are open, and the team closes about 10 per working day.
steps: Average cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 working days per ticket.
Funmi sets a WIP limit: no more than 15 tickets open in the team at once. New tickets wait in a queue and are pulled in strict priority order.
Closing speed stays about 10 per day, because the team size is unchanged.
New average cycle time = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 working days once a customer's ticket is started.
With less switching between tickets, many teams also find throughput rises a little, which shortens cycle time further.
blocks.result: Halving work in progress halved the time each opened ticket takes. Customers get answers faster without hiring more staff. The queue before the board still needs watching, which is why Funmi also reports total waiting time.

blocks.text: Little's Law only holds when the system is roughly stable, meaning items arrive and leave at about the same rate. If 20 new tickets arrive each day but only 10 are closed, the queue grows every day and no WIP limit can hide that. The honest fix is then a capacity conversation: more people, fewer channels, automated answers to common questions, or a clear statement of what the team will not handle.
Which approach for which work?

blocks.title: Choosing an approach
items: Scrum (complex, plannable)
Kanban with WIP limits
Plan-driven project plan
Simple Kanban list
axes: How predictable the incoming work is (left plannable, right interrupt-driven)
How uncertain the solution is (top high, bottom low)
blocks.caption: Uncertain work that can be planned in batches suits Scrum; constant, unpredictable arrivals suit Kanban.

head: Type of work
Better fit
Why
rows: Building a new app or website
Scrum
Uncertain solution; benefits from Sprint Goals and regular reviews with users
IT help desk or customer support
Kanban
Work arrives unpredictably every hour; two-week commitments break constantly
Constructing a borehole to a known design
Plan-driven
Well-understood steps; order is fixed by physics and permits
Marketing team running campaigns plus urgent requests
Hybrid (Scrum with a small Kanban lane for urgent work)
Planned campaigns plus interruptions that cannot wait

blocks.title: Hybrid is fine, if it is honest
blocks.text: Many teams run Sprints and also keep WIP limits on their board. That is a sensible mix. What is not sensible is calling a process "Scrum" while skipping Reviews and Retrospectives. Name what you really do.

A practical test: ask how many times last month urgent work forced the team to drop what it had planned. If the answer is "almost every week", Sprint commitments will keep breaking and Kanban, or a Scrum team with a fixed share of capacity kept free for urgent work, will serve better. If the answer is "rarely", Scrum's rhythm of goals, reviews and retrospectives usually brings more focus.
Where these skills are used

Scrum and Kanban are standard in software and digital product teams, including fintech, e-commerce and logistics startups across Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa and Egypt, and in the many international teams that hire remotely. They are also spreading to non-software work: NGO programme teams planning training cohorts in Sprints, content teams using Kanban boards, and banks running Agile transformation programmes. Roles that ask for this knowledge include Scrum Master, Agile Delivery Lead, Project Manager, Product Owner, and developers and designers who must work inside a Scrum Team.

blocks.title: Remote and low-data teams
blocks.text: Distributed teams run Scrum over Google Meet, Zoom or WhatsApp calls with a shared online board. On costly data, a 15-minute audio-only Daily Scrum with the board link shared in the group chat works well.

takeaways: Kanban has no Sprints; it visualises work and limits work in progress
Little's Law: cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput, so lower WIP means faster finishing
Scrum suits uncertain work that can be planned in batches; Kanban suits unpredictable arrivals
Honest hybrids are fine; a Scrum label without Reviews and Retrospectives is not

activity.title: Practice task: diagnose three kinds of work
steps: List three kinds of work from your life or job (for example, the WhatsApp orders for a small business, a website build, planning a wedding).
For each, note how predictable the incoming work is and how uncertain the solution is.
Decide Scrum, Kanban, plan-driven or hybrid for each, with one sentence of reasoning.
For one Kanban candidate, count current open items and items finished per day, and calculate cycle time with Little's Law.
activity.evidence: A short table of the three work types with your choice and the Little's Law calculation.

quiz.q: A manager says, "We are Agile now, so we no longer need any written plan." What is the best response?
options: He is right; the manifesto rejects plans
The manifesto values responding to change more than following a plan, but plans still have value and are updated often
Plans are only removed in Kanban, not Scrum
Agile requires a fixed one-year plan
quiz.explain: The manifesto says there is value in the items on the right (such as following a plan); Agile simply values responding to change more. Plans exist and are revised as the team learns.

quiz.q: In Scrum, who has the authority to cancel a Sprint?
options: Any stakeholder who attends the Sprint Review
quiz.explain: The Scrum Guide says only the Product Owner may cancel a Sprint, for example when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

quiz.q: What is the maximum timebox for the Daily Scrum?
quiz.explain: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers, held every working day of the Sprint.

quiz.q: Which commitment belongs to the Increment?
quiz.explain: Product Backlog has the Product Goal, Sprint Backlog has the Sprint Goal, and the Increment has the Definition of Done.

quiz.q: A team has 24 items in progress on average and finishes 8 per day. Using Little's Law, what is the average cycle time?
An IT help desk receives unpredictable requests all day. Which approach usually fits best?
quiz.explain: Constant, unpredictable arrivals break Sprint commitments; Kanban lets the team pull work as capacity frees up while limiting work in progress.

modules.title: Running Sprints: Backlog, Board, Events and Quality
modules.overview: This module is hands-on. You set up a Product Backlog and board in a real tool, run Sprint Planning with a capacity calculation, facilitate the Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective, and use a Definition of Done and a burndown chart to keep quality honest.

lessons.title: Setting up the Product Backlog, the board and a Definition of Done
objectives: Write and order Product Backlog items so the most valuable work sits at the top
Run a backlog refinement session and size items with relative estimates
Set up a Sprint board in Trello, Jira or a shared spreadsheet
Draft a Definition of Done that a team can actually check

blocks.text: Before the first Sprint, a Scrum Team needs three practical things: an ordered **Product Backlog**, a **board** where the Sprint's work is visible, and a written **Definition of Done**. This lesson sets up all three, using a realistic small project.
The Product Backlog: ordered, not just listed

The Product Backlog is owned by the Product Owner. It is a single list, **ordered** by what the Product Owner believes delivers the most value soonest, considering risk, cost and dependencies. Items at the top are small and clear enough to be done within one Sprint. Items lower down can be rough ideas. The Scrum Guide calls the ongoing work of splitting and clarifying items **refinement**.

items: Each item has a short title, a description of the need, and conditions that show when it is complete.
Items are written as outcomes for a user where possible, not as technical chores.
The order is visible to everyone, so nobody has to guess what comes next.
Refinement usually takes no more than about 10% of the team's time in a Sprint, a common guideline rather than a rule.

blocks.text: Sizing with relative estimates

Scrum does not tell you how to estimate. Many teams use **story points**, a relative size based on effort, complexity and uncertainty, often on the scale 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. A 5 is roughly two to three times a 2. A popular technique is **Planning Poker**: everyone reveals a number at the same time, the highest and lowest explain their thinking, and the team re-votes. The discussion is more valuable than the number, because it exposes hidden work.

blocks.name: task-list
blocks.alt: A person reviewing an ordered list of tasks
blocks.caption: An ordered backlog answers the question "what should we do next?" before anyone has to ask.

blocks.title: Worked example: a first backlog for a bakery ordering service
blocks.context: For example, a 5-person team is building a WhatsApp-based ordering system for Tola's bakery in Ibadan. Tola is the Product Owner. The Product Goal: customers can order and pay for cakes without a phone call.
steps: Brainstorm 9 items, then Tola orders them by value. Top 4: (1) customer sees the cake menu with prices, (2) customer places an order with pickup date, (3) customer pays by bank transfer and uploads proof, (4) Tola gets a daily list of orders.
Refinement: item 3 is too big, so the team splits it into 3a: show bank details and order reference, and 3b: Tola confirms payment and the customer gets a confirmation message.
Planning Poker sizes: item 1 = 3 points, item 2 = 5, item 3a = 2, item 3b = 5, item 4 = 3.
Total for the top five items = 3 + 5 + 2 + 5 + 3 = 18 points.
Lower items (loyalty discount, delivery tracking) stay rough and unsized for now.
blocks.result: The team has a refined, sized top of the backlog worth 18 points, enough for about one Sprint once their real speed is known. Card payment and delivery tracking wait until value is proven.

blocks.text: The board

blocks.title: A simple Sprint board
items: Sprint Backlog
In progress (WIP 3)
In review
Done (meets DoD)
blocks.caption: An item only moves to Done when every Definition of Done check is ticked.

head: Tool
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Trello
Small teams and non-software teams; simple lists and cards; free plan available
Few built-in Scrum reports; burndown needs a power-up or a sheet
Jira (Atlassian)
Software teams; built-in Scrum boards, sprints and reports; free plan for small teams
Can feel heavy; easy to over-configure
GitHub Projects
Teams whose code is already on GitHub
Less familiar to non-technical stakeholders
Google Sheets
Very low data and no new logins; anyone can open it
Manual updating; easy for the board to go stale

blocks.title: Protect customer data on boards
blocks.text: Never paste customers' phone numbers, account numbers, BVN or payment screenshots onto a board card. Board tools are shared widely and links get forwarded. Use an order reference instead, and keep personal data in the secured system, in line with Nigeria's data protection law (the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023).
The Definition of Done

The **Definition of Done (DoD)** is a formal description of the quality an Increment must meet. If an item does not meet it, it cannot be released or shown as done at the Sprint Review; it goes back to the Product Backlog. A good DoD is short, checkable and agreed by the whole team. For Tola's project, it could be:

items: Works on a low-cost Android phone and on a slow 3G connection
Tested by someone other than the person who built it
No customer personal data visible in logs or screenshots
Message wording checked by the Product Owner
How-to note updated in the shared folder

blocks.title: Start small, tighten later
blocks.text: A first DoD with five honest checks beats a list of twenty that nobody follows. Raise the bar at Retrospectives as the team improves.

takeaways: The Product Backlog is a single ordered list owned by the Product Owner
Refinement splits and clarifies items; relative estimates reveal hidden work
Pick a board tool your team will actually update
The Definition of Done is short, checkable and non-negotiable for calling work done

activity.title: Practice task: set up your backlog and board
steps: Choose a small real or mock product (for example, an online order form for a local business).
Write at least 8 backlog items and order them with the Product Goal in mind.
Split any item that feels too big for one Sprint, then size the top 5 with Planning Poker numbers (alone or with friends).
Create a free Trello board or a Google Sheet with the four columns from the diagram.
Write a Definition of Done with 4 to 6 checks.
activity.evidence: Screenshot of your board with ordered, sized items, plus your Definition of Done.

lessons.title: Facilitating the Sprint: planning by capacity, Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective
objectives: Calculate a team's capacity and forecast for a Sprint using past velocity
Write a clear Sprint Goal during Sprint Planning
Keep a Daily Scrum to 15 minutes and move problem-solving to after it
Facilitate a Sprint Review and a Retrospective that end in concrete actions

blocks.text: Knowing the events is not the same as running them well. This lesson is about facilitation: what the Scrum Master and team actually do in each event, with timings you can use tomorrow.
Sprint Planning: why, what, how

Sprint Planning answers three questions from the Scrum Guide. **Why** is this Sprint valuable? The team agrees a **Sprint Goal**, one sentence that gives the Sprint its purpose. **What** can be Done this Sprint? The Developers select items from the top of the backlog. **How** will the work get done? They break items into tasks, often a day or less each. The Developers decide how much they can take on; the Product Owner cannot force more in.

blocks.name: calendar
blocks.caption: Capacity starts with the calendar: holidays, leave and other duties all reduce what fits in a Sprint.

blocks.title: Worked example: capacity and forecast for a 2-week Sprint
blocks.context: For example, Chidi's team has 5 Developers and runs 10-working-day Sprints. One day in this Sprint is a public holiday, and Ada has 2 days of leave. Past Sprints delivered 21, 18 and 24 points.
steps: Available days: 5 people × 10 days = 50 person-days.
Subtract the holiday: 5 × 1 = 5 person-days, so 45 remain.
Subtract Ada's leave: 2 person-days, so 43 remain.
Capacity ratio = 43 ÷ 50 = 0.86, or 86% of a normal Sprint.
Average velocity = (21 + 18 + 24) ÷ 3 = 63 ÷ 3 = 21 points.
Forecast = 21 × 0.86 = 18.06, so about 18 points.
blocks.result: The team forecasts about 18 points, not 21. They pull items worth 18 points from the top of the backlog, write the Sprint Goal "Customers can pay by transfer and get confirmation", and plan tasks for the first few days.

head: Weak Sprint Goal
Stronger Sprint Goal
Why it is better
rows: Finish tickets 14 to 22
Customers can pay by transfer and get confirmation
Describes value, so the team can trade items and still meet it
Work on the reports module
The director can see last week's sales on her phone every Monday
Names a user and a checkable result
Do as much as possible
Test whether parents will book a fees reminder via WhatsApp
Gives a clear learning purpose for an uncertain idea

blocks.title: Velocity is a forecast tool, not a target
blocks.text: Velocity (points done per Sprint) is not in the Scrum Guide; it is a common complementary practice. Use it only to forecast your own team. Comparing velocity between teams, or rewarding higher numbers, makes teams inflate their estimates.
The Daily Scrum: 15 minutes, focused on the goal

The Daily Scrum is for the Developers. They look at the board and agree the plan for the next 24 hours toward the Sprint Goal. A useful format is to **walk the board from right to left**: start with items nearest Done and ask what is needed to finish them, then items in progress, then anything blocked. When a topic needs more than a minute, the Scrum Master says "let's take that after" and notes it. Those who need to stay remain for the follow-up; everyone else goes back to work.

For remote teams, keep the board on screen and let one Developer share it while others speak. On weak connections, switch cameras off and keep audio only. Start on time even if one person is late; the Daily Scrum belongs to those present.
The Sprint Review: a working session, not a slideshow

items: Product Owner restates the Sprint Goal and what was and was not Done (5 minutes).
Developers demonstrate the working Increment on a real device, ideally with a stakeholder using it (30 to 40 minutes).
Stakeholders give feedback; the Product Owner notes new or changed backlog items (30 minutes).
Group looks at what has changed in the market, budget or timeline, and discusses what to do next (20 minutes).

blocks.text: Invite the people who will use or pay for the product, not only managers. Ask open questions such as "what would stop you using this tomorrow?" rather than "do you like it?". Never demo work that is not Done; show it as in progress or leave it out.
The Sprint Retrospective: from talk to one change

blocks.title: A 90-minute Retrospective
items: Set the stage (10 min)
Gather data (20 min)
Generate insights (25 min)
Decide actions (20 min)
Close (15 min)
blocks.caption: This five-step shape, from Derby and Larsen's book Agile Retrospectives, stops the meeting turning into complaints.

head: Format
Prompts
Good when
rows: Start, Stop, Continue
What should we start doing, stop doing, continue doing?
New teams; quick and easy to explain
Mad, Sad, Glad
What made you mad, sad or glad this Sprint?
Feelings are running high and need airing
4Ls
Liked, Learned, Lacked, Longed for
You want learning and missing support to surface
Sailboat
Wind (helps us), anchors (slow us), rocks (risks ahead), island (goal)
Bigger-picture or remote teams using a visual board

blocks.text: End every Retrospective with **one or two** specific improvement actions, each with an owner and a check date. The Scrum Guide notes that the most impactful improvements can be added to the next Sprint Backlog. One done action is worth more than ten good ideas left on sticky notes.

takeaways: Sprint Planning produces a Sprint Goal, selected items and a plan
Forecast with average velocity adjusted for real capacity
Keep the Daily Scrum to 15 minutes; solve problems after it
Every Retrospective ends with one or two owned, dated actions

activity.title: Practice task: run a mini-Sprint
steps: Using the board from the previous lesson, calculate your capacity for a 1-week Sprint (count holidays and other duties honestly).
Hold Sprint Planning (even alone or with 2 friends): write a Sprint Goal and pull items that fit the forecast.
Hold a 15-minute Daily Scrum at least 3 times during the week, walking the board right to left.
End the week with a short Review (show what works) and a Start, Stop, Continue Retrospective.
Record one improvement action with an owner and a date.
activity.evidence: Your capacity calculation, Sprint Goal, a board screenshot at the end, and the Retrospective notes with the action.

lessons.title: Keeping Scrum honest: burndown charts, healthy signals and common anti-patterns
objectives: Read a Sprint burndown chart and decide when to act
Recognise the most common Scrum anti-patterns and their fixes
Keep light, useful records: Sprint Goals, Review notes and a Retrospective action log
Adapt Scrum practices without losing the parts that make it work

blocks.text: Many organisations perform Scrum events without getting Scrum's benefits. People call this **"Scrum in name only"** or cargo-cult Scrum. Your job, especially as a Scrum Master, is to notice the warning signs early, using data and honest conversation, not blame.
Reading a burndown chart

A **Sprint burndown chart** plots the work remaining (in points, tasks or hours) against the days of the Sprint. An **ideal line** runs straight from the total on day 0 to zero on the last day. The **actual line** shows reality. Burndowns are not required by Scrum, but they are a simple, popular way to make progress transparent.

blocks.name: chart-with-downwards-trend
blocks.alt: A chart with a line trending downward
blocks.caption: A healthy burndown slopes down steadily; a flat line in the first half of the Sprint is a signal to act.

blocks.title: Worked example: spotting trouble on day 5
blocks.context: For example, Halima's team planned 40 points in a 10-day Sprint. On the evening of day 5 the chart shows 34 points remaining.
steps: Ideal burn rate = 40 ÷ 10 = 4 points per day.
Ideal remaining at day 5 = 40 − (5 × 4) = 20 points.
Actual remaining = 34 points, so the team is 34 − 20 = 14 points behind the ideal line.
Actual rate so far = (40 − 34) ÷ 5 = 1.2 points per day. At that rate, the last 5 days would finish only 6 more points, leaving 28 undone.
At the next Daily Scrum, Halima asks what is blocking work. The team finds three items all waiting for one API key from a partner bank.
The Developers and Product Owner agree to escalate the key that morning, and the Product Owner renegotiates scope: an 8-point item that does not serve the Sprint Goal goes back to the backlog.
blocks.result: The chart did not fix anything by itself; it started the right conversation on day 5 instead of day 10. Scope was adjusted with the Product Owner while keeping the Sprint Goal, which the Scrum Guide allows.

blocks.text: Signals of a healthy Scrum Team

blocks.title: Healthy Sprint signals
items: Sprint Goal known by everyone
Daily Scrum ends in 15 minutes
Review shows working product
Done means meets the DoD
Retro actions actually completed
Product Owner reachable daily
blocks.caption: If three or more of these are missing, the team is likely doing Scrum in name only.

blocks.text: Common anti-patterns and what to do

head: Anti-pattern
Why it hurts
What to try
rows: Daily Scrum becomes a status report to the manager
Developers stop owning the plan; meeting runs long
Manager listens only or leaves; walk the board, not the people
Work keeps being added mid-Sprint
Sprint Goal is lost; team never finishes
All new requests go to the Product Owner, who decides; urgent items swap out something of equal size
Items carried over Sprint after Sprint
Forecasts become meaningless
Split items smaller; plan less; strengthen refinement
Retrospective with no follow-up
Team stops believing it can change anything
Review last Sprint's actions first, every time
Absent Product Owner
Developers guess, then rework
Agree a daily availability window; name a delegate for questions only
Velocity used to rank teams
Estimates inflate; trust drops
Report outcomes and Sprint Goals met instead

blocks.title: Psychological safety comes first
blocks.text: If people fear blame, Retrospectives turn into "everything was fine". Use the Prime Directive from Norm Kerth's work on retrospectives: assume everyone did the best job they could with what they knew at the time. For sensitive teams, collect input anonymously first, for example with a Google Form.
Better measures than velocity alone

head: Measure
How to calculate
What it tells you
rows: Sprint Goal success rate
Sprints where the goal was met ÷ total Sprints, over the last 6
Whether the team delivers on its purpose, not just its points
Carry-over rate
Points not Done ÷ points planned, per Sprint
Whether planning is realistic; aim to bring it down over time
Cycle time
Days from starting an item to Done, averaged
How quickly value reaches users; long times point to waiting or oversized items
Escaped defects
Problems found by users after release, per Sprint
Whether the Definition of Done is strong enough

blocks.text: For example, if a team met its Sprint Goal in 4 of its last 6 Sprints, the success rate is 4 ÷ 6 = 67%. Track two or three measures at most, review them at the Retrospective, and look at trends over several Sprints rather than reacting to one bad week.
Light documentation that pays off

items: **Sprint log**: one line per Sprint with dates, Sprint Goal, met or not met, points done.
**Review notes**: who attended, main feedback, backlog changes agreed.
**Retrospective action log**: action, owner, due date, done or not. Review it at the start of each Retrospective.
**Definition of Done history**: note each time the team raised the bar and why.

blocks.text: These four records take about 15 minutes per Sprint and give you real evidence for your portfolio later in this course. Store them in one shared folder.

blocks.title: Adapting Scrum, carefully
blocks.text: Changing practices around Scrum, such as estimation style, board columns or Retrospective format, is normal. Removing an event, an artifact or an accountability means you are no longer doing Scrum, and the Scrum Guide says so. Be clear which kind of change you are making.

takeaways: A burndown compares actual remaining work with an ideal line; act early when it flattens
Most problems show up as long Daily Scrums, mid-Sprint scope changes and carried-over work
Scope may be renegotiated with the Product Owner, but the Sprint Goal is protected
Four light records give the team memory and give you portfolio evidence

activity.title: Practice task: health check your mini-Sprint
steps: Draw a burndown for your mini-Sprint from the last lesson (paper or Google Sheets line chart).
Calculate the ideal line and mark the day the actual line was furthest from it.
Score your Sprint against the six healthy signals in the checklist.
Pick the weakest signal and write one fix from the anti-patterns table.
Start your Sprint log and Retrospective action log in one shared document.
activity.evidence: Burndown chart image, the six-signal score, and the first entries of your Sprint log and action log.

quiz.q: A team averages 20 points per Sprint. Next Sprint they have 80% of their usual capacity because of holidays. What is a sensible forecast?
quiz.explain: Forecast = average velocity × capacity ratio = 20 × 0.8 = 16 points.

quiz.q: During the Daily Scrum, two Developers start a detailed debate about database design. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Let it run; technical talk is valuable
Note the topic and ask them to continue right after the 15-minute Daily Scrum
quiz.explain: The Daily Scrum is timeboxed to 15 minutes and focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal; deeper problem-solving happens straight after with the people who need to be there.

quiz.q: An item was built but not tested, which the Definition of Done requires. What happens at the Sprint Review?
options: It is shown as done because the code exists
It is not presented as part of the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog
The Scrum Master tests it during the Review
The Sprint is extended by a week
quiz.explain: Work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

quiz.q: A 30-point, 10-day Sprint has 27 points left on day 5. How far behind the ideal line is the team?
quiz.explain: Ideal remaining on day 5 = 30 − (5 × 3) = 15. Actual is 27, so the team is 27 − 15 = 12 points behind.

quiz.q: A department head asks for a new urgent feature in the middle of a Sprint. What is the healthiest response?
options: Developers add it immediately and work overtime
The Scrum Master refuses all requests until the next quarter
The request goes to the Product Owner, who decides whether it is worth swapping out work of similar size without endangering the Sprint Goal
quiz.explain: The Product Owner owns ordering and scope decisions. Scope can be renegotiated within the Sprint, but the Sprint Goal should be protected.

options: A list of 12 ideas on sticky notes
No actions because everything went fine
One action: "Product Owner holds a 30-minute Q&A window daily at 11:00, owner Bisi, check at next Retro"
quiz.explain: Effective Retrospectives end with one or two specific actions with an owner and a check date.

modules.title: Coaching Teams, Consulting and Your Agile Career
modules.overview: You learn to diagnose a team that wants to work in an Agile way, to scope and price Scrum Master or coaching work and protect that scope, and to turn your practice into a certification path, an evidence portfolio and a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Diagnosing a team: discovery questions and a Scrum health check
objectives: Prepare discovery questions across process, people, tools and leadership
Run a scored Scrum health check with a team
Choose the two improvements that will make the biggest difference first
Explain psychological safety and how to protect it during discovery

blocks.text: Whether you are joining a team as Scrum Master or invited in as a coach, your first job is not to teach Scrum. It is to **understand what is really happening**. Teams that say "Scrum does not work here" are often running a version with key parts missing. Teams that say "we do Scrum perfectly" sometimes hide serious problems. Discovery gives you evidence before you suggest anything.
Four areas to ask about

head: Area
Questions to ask
What you are listening for
rows: Process
Walk me through your last Sprint from planning to Retrospective. What was the Sprint Goal? Was it met?
Missing events, no Sprint Goal, carried-over work
People
When did someone last raise a problem in a Retrospective? What happened next?
Fear, silence, blame, or actions that never happen
Tools and data
Show me your board. When was it last updated? How do you know the Sprint is on track?
Stale boards, no Definition of Done, no shared measure of progress
Leadership and organisation
Who can add work to the team? How are deadlines set? How is the team's performance judged?
Many people pushing work directly, fixed scope with fixed dates, velocity used as a target

blocks.text: Ask the same questions to several people separately: the Product Owner, two or three Developers, and the manager who sponsors the team. Differences between their answers are often the most useful finding. Observe at least one Daily Scrum and one Review or Retrospective in person or on the call, without speaking.

items: **When observing a Daily Scrum**, note the start and end times, who speaks most, whether the Sprint Goal is mentioned, and whether anyone reports to a manager rather than to the team.
**When observing a Review**, note whether real users attend, whether working product is shown, and whether the backlog changes as a result.
**When looking at the board**, count items in progress per person and items older than one Sprint.
**Write facts, not judgements**: "Daily Scrum lasted 34 minutes; the manager asked each person for status" rather than "the meeting was bad".

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people in a one-to-one conversation
blocks.caption: Short one-to-one conversations surface issues people will not raise in a group.

blocks.title: Psychological safety
blocks.text: Harvard professor Amy Edmondson describes psychological safety as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, such as admitting mistakes or asking questions. During discovery, promise that individual comments will not be quoted with names, and keep that promise.
The scored health check

After the interviews, run a 45-minute health check with the whole team. Each person scores eight statements from 1 (not true at all) to 5 (completely true), anonymously, for example with a Google Form. You then show the averages and discuss the lowest two.

items: We have a clear Sprint Goal and everyone knows it.
Our Product Owner is available when we need decisions.
Our Daily Scrum helps us and ends on time.
We finish what we start in a Sprint.
Our Definition of Done is clear and we follow it.
Stakeholders see working results at every Review.
Retrospective actions really get done.
I feel safe raising problems in this team.

blocks.title: Discovery to first improvement
items: One-to-one interviews
Observe real events
Anonymous health check
Pick lowest two areas
Agree experiments with team
blocks.caption: Evidence first, then the team chooses what to change; the coach does not impose fixes.

blocks.title: Worked example: health check for an NGO training team
blocks.context: For example, a 7-person programme team at a women's empowerment NGO in Enugu plans and delivers online training cohorts in 2-week Sprints. Kemi, their new Scrum Master, runs the health check. All 7 respond.
steps: Statement 4 (we finish what we start) scores: 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 2. Total = 15. Average = 15 ÷ 7 = 2.14.
Statement 2 (Product Owner available) scores: 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 1. Total = 13. Average = 13 ÷ 7 = 1.86.
Statement 8 (safe to raise problems) averages 4.3, so safety is not the main issue.
Interviews explain the low scores: the programme director, who is Product Owner, is often travelling, and donors' requests go straight to individual staff.
With the team, Kemi agrees two experiments for the next two Sprints: a named deputy who can answer day-to-day questions, and a rule that all new requests go onto the backlog first.
Success measure: both averages rise above 3 at the next health check in four weeks.
blocks.result: The team works on two specific, measured problems instead of "doing Scrum better" in general. The lowest scores pointed straight at the cause: decisions and incoming work were not flowing through the Product Owner.

blocks.title: Report the findings carefully
blocks.text: Share the summary with the team first, then with the sponsor. Present patterns and averages, never "Tunde said". Lead with one thing the team does well; it makes the hard findings easier to accept.

takeaways: Understand before you teach: interview, observe, then measure
Ask about process, people, tools and leadership separately
An anonymous scored health check turns opinions into comparable numbers
Pick the lowest two areas and agree measurable experiments with the team

activity.title: Practice task: run a mini health check
steps: Choose a team you know: workplace, church unit, cooperative, volunteer group or study group.
Interview two members for 10 minutes each using two questions from each area in the table.
Put the eight health-check statements into a free Google Form and ask at least four members to score them.
Calculate the average for each statement and identify the lowest two.
Write one experiment for each low area with a success measure and a review date.
activity.evidence: Your interview notes (no names), a screenshot of the form results, and your two experiments.

lessons.title: Scrum Master and coaching work: engagement types, proposals and protecting scope
objectives: Distinguish employed Scrum roles from consulting and coaching engagements
Write a short proposal that states outcomes, activities, exclusions and duration
Compare a fixed package with a monthly retainer using simple arithmetic
Handle scope changes with a written change note

blocks.text: Most people use Scrum skills inside a job: as a Scrum Master, delivery lead, project manager, Product Owner, or as a developer or designer on a Scrum Team. Some experienced practitioners also do **independent work**: training teams, coaching a Scrum Master, or helping a whole department adopt Agile ways of working. This lesson covers how to define and protect that kind of engagement.
Three common engagement types

head: Engagement
Typical activities
Typical shape
rows: Team kick-off
Health check, one or two days of training, help with the first Sprint Planning and Retrospective
Short fixed package, a few weeks
Interim or part-time Scrum Master
Facilitates all events, removes impediments, coaches the Product Owner, trains a successor
Monthly retainer, several months
Agile coaching for a department
Works with several teams and their managers on structure, roles, metrics and leadership habits
Longer engagement, phased, with review points

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a signed contract document
blocks.caption: A one-page written scope protects both you and the client when requests grow.

blocks.text: Setting a day rate you can live on

Independent consultants are not paid for every working day. Time goes to finding clients, preparing training, travel, invoicing and learning. A simple way to set a rate is: monthly income you need (including tax, pension, data, transport and tools) ÷ the number of days you can realistically bill in a month. If you need ₦1,000,000 a month and can bill about 12 days, your floor is about ₦83,000 per day. Then check it against what similar roles earn locally and what value the client expects. Never price from guesswork alone; ask peers, read job adverts and keep records of what clients accept.
What a short proposal contains

items: **Situation**: two or three sentences from your discovery, in the client's own words where possible.
**Outcomes**: what will be different, with measures (for example, Sprint Goals met in at least 3 of the last 4 Sprints).
**Activities**: exactly what you will do, how often and with whom.
**Exclusions**: what is not included (for example, coaching additional teams, writing software, HR decisions).
**Duration and review points**: start date, end date, and a mid-point review.
**Fees and payment terms**: amount, schedule, and how changes are handled.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixed package or retainer?
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma is an experienced Scrum Master. A Port Harcourt software firm wants help for one team. She decides her day rate from her own costs and income target; here we use ₦80,000 per day as an illustrative figure, not a market rate.
steps: Option A, fixed kick-off package: 3 days discovery and health check + 2 days training + 4 half-days supporting events = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 days. Fee = 7 × ₦80,000 = ₦560,000.
Option B, part-time Scrum Master for 3 months at 2 days per week: about 2 × 4 = 8 days a month. Monthly retainer = 8 × ₦80,000 = ₦640,000. Three months = ₦1,920,000.
She offers Option B at a small commitment discount of 10% for paying monthly in advance: ₦640,000 × 0.9 = ₦576,000 per month, ₦1,728,000 in total.
Halfway through, the client asks her to add a second team. Her change note: 1 extra day per week for the remaining 6 weeks = 6 days × ₦80,000 = ₦480,000, with a revised end-of-engagement review.
The client signs the change note before the extra work starts.
blocks.result: Both options and the change are priced from the same day rate, so the client can compare them easily. The written change note means the second team is extra paid work, not free scope creep.

blocks.title: In scope versus out of scope
items: In scope (Option B)
Out of scope unless agreed
blocks.caption: Writing exclusions down is what makes a change note possible later.

blocks.title: Payment and scam safety
blocks.text: Use a written agreement and invoices for every engagement. Request a deposit before starting for new clients. Be wary of overseas "clients" who overpay and ask for a refund of the difference, or who ask you to pay for software or training before they hire you; these are known scam patterns. Receive payments through your business bank account or a recognised processor such as Paystack.

items: **Name the decision-maker**: one client contact who can approve change notes and sign off milestones.
**Agree how you will measure success** before you start, using numbers from your health check.
**Plan your exit**: from the first month, train someone inside the team to carry on, so the client does not depend on you forever.
**Keep a short weekly note** of what you did and what changed; it supports your invoice and your portfolio.

blocks.text: Finally, be honest about what Scrum can and cannot fix. If the real problem is that leadership sets fixed scope and fixed dates without listening to the team, say so early. A good coach protects the client's money by naming the real constraint, even when it is uncomfortable.

takeaways: Most Scrum work is employed; independent work is usually kick-offs, interim Scrum Master roles or coaching
A proposal states outcomes, activities, exclusions, duration and fees
Price every option and every change from the same day rate
Exclusions and signed change notes are how you control scope

activity.title: Practice task: write a one-page proposal
steps: Use your health-check findings from the previous lesson as the Situation.
Write two or three measurable Outcomes and the Activities that will achieve them.
List at least four Exclusions.
Choose your own day rate (base it on your costs and income goal) and price a fixed package and a retainer option.
Draft a sample change note for one likely extra request.
activity.evidence: A one-page proposal with both price options and a sample change note.

lessons.title: Certifications, an evidence portfolio and your 90-day plan
objectives: Compare the main entry-level Scrum certifications and how to prepare
Build a short case study from your own Sprint evidence
Write interview answers that show real Scrum judgement
Create a 90-day plan with weekly, checkable actions

blocks.text: Employers and clients want two things: proof you understand Scrum correctly, and proof you have used it. A certification helps with the first. A small, honest portfolio of real practice helps with the second, and often counts for more.
Entry-level certifications

head: Certification
Issued by
How you get it
Good to know
rows: Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I)
Scrum.org (founded by Ken Schwaber)
Pass an online assessment; no course required
Study the Scrum Guide closely and use the free Scrum Open practice assessment
Certified ScrumMaster (CSM)
Scrum Alliance
Attend a course with a Certified Scrum Trainer, then pass the exam
Course includes live practice; needs renewal with education units
Professional Scrum Product Owner I (PSPO I)
Scrum.org
Pass an online assessment
Useful if you aim for Product Owner work

blocks.title: Check fees and rules on the official sites
blocks.text: Fees, exam length, passing scores and renewal rules change over time and vary by country and trainer. Always check scrum.org and scrumalliance.org directly before you pay, and pay only on those official sites or a trainer they list.
How to prepare for a Scrum assessment

items: Read the Scrum Guide slowly, twice. It is short, and most exam questions test its exact wording, such as "accountabilities", "commitments" and who owns which decision.
After each section, write one line in your own words. Note anything that surprised you, such as the Product Owner being one person.
Take the free practice assessments on scrum.org repeatedly until you score well consistently, and read the explanation for every wrong answer.
Watch for trick wording: "must", "always" and "only". If the Scrum Guide does not say it, Scrum does not require it.
Join a study group, for example a WhatsApp group of 3 or 4 learners, and quiz each other on scenarios.

blocks.name: certification
blocks.caption: A certification proves understanding; your Sprint evidence proves practice.

blocks.text: Your evidence portfolio

You already have material from this course: a Sprint calendar, a backlog and board, a mini-Sprint with a burndown, a Retrospective action log, a health check and a proposal. Turn the best of it into a **one-page case study** using this structure:

items: **Context**: team, product or programme, and your role (be honest if it was a practice or volunteer project).
**Problem**: what was not working, with a number if you have one.
**What you did**: the Scrum practices you introduced or facilitated.
**Result**: what changed, with before-and-after numbers.
**What you learned**: one thing you would do differently.

blocks.title: Worked example: case study numbers from a volunteer team
blocks.context: For example, Zainab volunteers with a church youth unit that runs a monthly outreach event. She introduced 2-week Sprints, a Trello board and Retrospectives for three months.
steps: Before: over the 3 events before Scrum, 21 tasks were planned and 12 were done on time. On-time rate = 12 ÷ 21 = 57%.
After: over the next 3 events, 24 tasks were planned and 20 were done on time. On-time rate = 20 ÷ 24 = 83%.
Improvement = 83 − 57 = 26 percentage points.
Retrospective actions: 6 agreed, 5 completed, so 5 ÷ 6 = 83% followed through.
Her case study headline: "Raised on-time task completion from 57% to 83% in three months by introducing Sprints, a visible board and action-focused Retrospectives."
blocks.result: A volunteer project with honest, simple numbers gives an interviewer something concrete to ask about, which is far stronger than listing "knowledge of Scrum" on a CV.

blocks.text: Interview questions to practise

items: "A stakeholder keeps adding work mid-Sprint. What do you do?" (Route it to the Product Owner; protect the Sprint Goal.)
"The Daily Scrum always runs 40 minutes. How would you fix it?" (Walk the board; move problem-solving after; check who is attending and why.)
"Your team's velocity dropped by a third. What does that tell you?" (Nothing by itself; look at capacity, item size, blockers and quality before judging.)
"What is the difference between Agile and Scrum?" (Values and principles versus one framework that applies them.)

blocks.title: A 90-day plan
items: Days 1-30: Scrum Guide, practice tests
Days 31-60: run Sprints, log evidence
Days 61-75: certification exam
Days 76-90: case study, applications
blocks.caption: Each phase produces something you can show, not just something you studied.

blocks.text: Make each week's action checkable: "read the Scrum Guide twice and summarise each section in one line", "score 90% or more on three practice tests in a row", "facilitate two Retrospectives", "send five tailored applications". Search LinkedIn and Jobberman for "Scrum Master", "Agile delivery" and "project manager Scrum" to see which skills appear most in the roles you want, and adjust your plan to match.

blocks.title: Avoid certification and job scams
blocks.text: Be careful with anyone who guarantees a job after a paid certificate, sells "exam dumps", or asks for payment through a personal account. Official certificates can be verified on the issuer's website; genuine employers do not charge you to apply.

takeaways: PSM I needs an online assessment; CSM needs a course with a Certified Scrum Trainer
Always check current fees and rules on the official sites
A one-page case study with honest numbers beats a list of buzzwords
A 90-day plan should produce evidence every month

activity.title: Practice task: case study and 90-day plan
steps: Pick your best piece of Sprint evidence from this course.
Write a one-page case study using Context, Problem, What you did, Result, What you learned.
Choose your target: a certification, a role, or Scrum as a supporting skill in your current job.
Write a 90-day plan with one checkable action per week.
Record yourself answering two of the interview questions and listen back once.
activity.evidence: Your case study, your 90-day plan, and a note of what you will improve in your interview answers.

quiz.q: A new Scrum Master hears from a manager that "the team does Scrum perfectly". What should she do first?
options: Accept it and start coaching other teams
Interview several team members separately and observe real events before suggesting changes
quiz.explain: Discovery comes first: one-to-one interviews and observation reveal what is really happening and where accounts differ.

quiz.q: A health-check statement gets scores of 3, 2, 4, 1 and 2 from five people. What is the average?
Using a day rate of ₦70,000 (illustrative), what is the fee for a change note covering 1 extra day per week for 5 weeks?
Which proposal element makes it easiest to handle a client's extra request later?
options: A list of your past clients
quiz.explain: Written exclusions show what was not agreed, so additional work can be priced through a change note instead of absorbed as scope creep.

quiz.q: Which statement about entry-level certifications is accurate?
options: PSM I requires a two-day course
Both are issued by the Project Management Institute
PSM I is earned by passing an online assessment without a required course
quiz.explain: Scrum.org's PSM I is an online assessment with no required course; the CSM from Scrum Alliance requires a course with a Certified Scrum Trainer.

quiz.q: In a case study, tasks done on time rose from 10 of 20 to 18 of 24. What is the improvement in percentage points?

finalQuiz.q: Which pair correctly matches Agile and Scrum?
options: Agile is a framework; Scrum is a set of values
Agile is a set of values and principles; Scrum is one framework that applies them
They are two names for the same thing
Scrum is a type of Kanban
finalQuiz.explain: The Agile Manifesto sets out values and principles; Scrum is a specific lightweight framework built on them.

finalQuiz.q: A team builds for 6 months before users see anything, then finds a wrong assumption. Which Agile idea would most reduce this risk?
options: Delivering working pieces every few weeks and inspecting them with users
finalQuiz.explain: Frequent working deliveries let the team inspect and adapt early, so wrong assumptions are found when they are cheap to fix.

finalQuiz.q: What is the maximum timebox of Sprint Planning for a one-month Sprint?
finalQuiz.explain: The Scrum Guide sets Sprint Planning at a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint; shorter Sprints usually need less.

finalQuiz.q: Who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog?
finalQuiz.explain: The Product Owner is accountable for Product Backlog management, including ordering it.

finalQuiz.q: A Kanban team has 40 items in progress and finishes 5 per day. What is the average cycle time?
finalQuiz.explain: Little's Law: cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 days.

finalQuiz.q: Velocity has averaged 30 points. Next Sprint the team has 70% of normal capacity. What is a sensible forecast?
Which item belongs in a Definition of Done?
options: "Tested by someone other than the builder"
finalQuiz.explain: A Definition of Done is a short list of specific, checkable quality criteria that every Increment must meet.

finalQuiz.q: In a 20-point, 10-day Sprint, 18 points remain on day 6. How far behind the ideal line is the team?
finalQuiz.explain: Ideal remaining on day 6 = 20 − (6 × 2) = 8. Actual is 18, so the team is 10 points behind.

finalQuiz.q: Retrospectives keep producing ideas but nothing changes. What should the Scrum Master try first?
options: Review last Sprint's actions at the start of each Retrospective and limit new actions to one or two with owners and dates
Ask the manager to choose the actions
finalQuiz.explain: Following up previous actions and committing to a small number of owned, dated actions is what turns Retrospectives into change.

finalQuiz.q: In a health check, "Our Product Owner is available" averages 1.9 out of 5. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore it, because scores are subjective
Explore the cause in interviews and agree a measurable experiment with the team, such as a daily Q&A window
finalQuiz.explain: Low scores point to where to look; the coach investigates the cause and agrees an experiment with a success measure.

finalQuiz.q: Halfway through an engagement, a client asks a coach to support a second team. What should she do?
options: Do it for free to keep the client happy
Write a priced change note and start only after the client agrees it
Reduce time on the first team without telling anyone
finalQuiz.explain: Extra work outside the written scope is handled with a priced change note agreed before the work starts.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the strongest portfolio evidence for a Scrum Master application?
options: "Good knowledge of Agile" on a CV
A list of Scrum terms memorised
A one-page case study showing on-time completion rising from 57% to 83% after introducing Sprints and Retrospectives
A screenshot of an online course homepage
finalQuiz.explain: Concrete, honest before-and-after evidence of practice is what employers and clients can ask about and trust.

capstone.title: Agile Practice Documentation Project
capstone.brief: Produce a practice pack that shows you understand Agile and Scrum correctly and can run them: a written explanation of the principles, roles, events and artifacts; documented evidence of a real or mock Sprint you facilitated, including planning and a Retrospective; and a 90-day plan toward your target opportunity.
steps: Write a 1 to 2 page explanation, in your own words, of the Agile values, Scrum's three accountabilities, five events and three artifacts with their commitments.
Set up a backlog, board and Definition of Done for a real or mock team of at least 3 people.
Run one Sprint of 1 or 2 weeks: Sprint Planning with a capacity calculation and Sprint Goal, at least three Daily Scrums, a Review and a Retrospective.
Record a burndown chart, a Sprint log entry and the Retrospective actions with owners.
Run the eight-statement health check with the team and write two experiments for the lowest scores.
Write a one-page case study and a 90-day plan naming your target role or certification and weekly actions.
evidence: Written explanation of Agile and Scrum (1 to 2 pages)
Board screenshot and Definition of Done
Sprint Planning notes with capacity calculation and Sprint Goal
Retrospective notes with one or two owned, dated actions
